questions.question: A set is best defined as:
options: any well-defined list, collection or class of objects
questions.explanation: A set is any well-defined list, collection or class of objects. “Well-defined” means we can decide clearly whether an object belongs to it or not.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a well-defined set?
options: The vowels of the English alphabet
questions.explanation: “Beautiful” is a matter of opinion, so membership cannot be decided clearly. The other three have clear membership rules.

questions.question: Sets are usually denoted by:
questions.explanation: By convention, sets are written with capital letters (A, B, X, Y, …) and their elements with lower-case letters.

questions.question: Write A = { x | x<sup>2</sup> = 4 } in tabular form.
questions.explanation: x2 = 4 gives x = 2 or x = −2. Hence A = {2, −2}.

questions.question: Write B = { x | x − 2 = 5 } in tabular form.
questions.explanation: x − 2 = 5 gives x = 5 + 2 = 7. Hence B = {7}.

questions.question: The set C = { x | x is positive and x is negative } is:
questions.explanation: No number is both positive and negative, so C has no elements: C = ∅.

questions.question: Write D = { x | x is a letter in the word “correct” } in tabular form.
options: {c, o, r, r, e, c, t}
questions.explanation: The letters of “correct” are c, o, r, r, e, c, t. A set does not repeat elements, so D = {c, o, r, e, t}.

questions.question: The set-builder form of {2, 4, 6, 8, …} is:
options: { x | x is even and positive }
questions.explanation: The elements are the positive even numbers, so the set is { x | x is even and x > 0 }.

questions.question: The symbol ∈ is read as:
questions.explanation: x ∈ A means “x belongs to A” (x is an element of A).

questions.question: If A = {a, e, i, o, u}, which statement is true?
questions.explanation: e is one of the elements of A, so e ∈ A. a and u are in A; b is not.

questions.question: If B = { x | x is an even number }, which statement is true?
questions.explanation: 14 is even, so 14 ∈ B. 3 and 11 are odd, and 6 is even so 6 ∈ B.

questions.question: Which of the following sets is finite?
options: { x | x is an even number }
{ x | x is a positive integer }
questions.explanation: The months of the year number 12; counting ends. The other sets never stop.

questions.question: Which of the following sets is infinite?
questions.explanation: The even numbers continue without end, so the counting never finishes. The other sets are finite.

questions.question: The set of all rivers on the earth is:
questions.explanation: Although hard to count in practice, the number of rivers is a definite number, so the set is finite.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 1, 4, 2}, then:
questions.explanation: They have exactly the same elements; order does not matter. So A = B.

questions.question: Which pair of sets is equal?
options: {r, t, s} and {s, t, r, s}
questions.explanation: Repeating an element does not change a set. Both sets contain exactly r, s and t.

questions.question: If E = { x | x<sup>2</sup> − 3x = −2 }, then E equals:
The symbol for the null (empty) set is:
questions.explanation: The empty set, with no elements, is written ∅.

questions.question: Which of the following is the empty set?
options: { x | x<sup>2</sup> = 4 and x is odd }
questions.explanation: x<sup>2</sup> = 4 gives x = ±2, neither of which is odd, so the set has no elements. {0} and {∅} each have one element.

questions.question: Which word has a different meaning from the others: empty, void, zero, null?
questions.explanation: Empty, void and null all describe a set with no elements. Zero is a number.

questions.question: A ⊂ B means:
options: every element of B is in A
every element of A is in B
A and B have no elements
questions.explanation: A is a subset of B when every element of A is also an element of B.

questions.question: If C = {1, 3, 5} and D = {5, 4, 3, 2, 1}, then:
questions.explanation: 1, 3 and 5 all belong to D, so C ⊂ D. D has elements (2, 4) not in C, so D ⊄ C and C ≠ D.

questions.question: The null set is:
options: not a subset of any set
a subset of non-empty sets only
questions.explanation: ∅ has no element that could fail to be in another set, so ∅ ⊂ A for every set A.

questions.question: Every set is a subset of:
questions.explanation: Every element of A is in A, so A ⊂ A.

questions.question: Two sets A and B are equal if and only if:
questions.explanation: Equality means the sets contain exactly the same elements, i.e. each is a subset of the other.

questions.question: B ⊃ A is read as:
options: B is a superset of A
B is not a subset of A
A is a member of B
questions.explanation: B ⊃ A means B contains A, i.e. B is a superset of A.

questions.question: If A ⊄ B, then:
options: at least one element of A is not in B
questions.explanation: A ⊂ B fails exactly when some element of A is missing from B.

questions.question: B is a proper subset of A if:
questions.explanation: A proper subset is a subset that is not equal to the whole set.

questions.question: How many subsets does a set with 4 elements have?
questions.explanation: A set with n elements has 2n subsets: 24 = 16.

questions.question: The power set of M = {a, b} is:
questions.explanation: The power set is the set of all subsets: {a, b}, {a}, {b} and ∅. So {{a, b}, {a}, {b}, ∅}.

questions.question: If S has 5 elements, the number of elements in its power set is:
Which of the following is a member of the power set of T = {4, 7, 8}?
questions.explanation: Members of the power set are subsets of T. {4, 8} ⊂ T, so it is a member. 4 is an element, not a subset.

questions.question: Two sets A and B are comparable if:
questions.explanation: Comparable means one of the sets is a subset of the other.

questions.question: Which pair of sets is NOT comparable?
questions.explanation: a is in {a, b} but not in {b, c, d}, and c is in {b, c, d} but not in {a, b}. Neither is a subset of the other.

questions.question: If A ⊂ B and B ⊂ C, then:
questions.explanation: Let x ∈ A. Then x ∈ B (as A ⊂ B), and then x ∈ C (as B ⊂ C). So every element of A is in C, i.e. A ⊂ C.

questions.question: Which of the following is a family (class) of sets?
questions.explanation: Every member of {{2,3},{2},{5,6}} is itself a set. In the others, some members are not sets.

questions.question: The universal set (universe of discourse) is usually denoted by:
questions.explanation: The universal set is denoted by U.

questions.question: Which pair of sets is disjoint?
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets have no common element. The other pairs share 7, 3 and b respectively.

questions.question: If A ⊂ B and A ≠ B, a Venn diagram can show this as:
options: circle A drawn inside circle B
circle B drawn inside circle A
questions.explanation: Since A is a subset of B, circle A is drawn inside circle B.

questions.question: In the axiomatic development of set theory, the undefined terms are:
questions.explanation: “Element” and “set” are undefined terms; “an element belongs to a set” is the undefined relation.

questions.question: The union of two sets A and B is the set of elements that belong to:
questions.explanation: A ∪ B = { x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B }.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then A ∪ B =
questions.explanation: Put all elements together, listing each once: {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8}.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then A ∪ C =
questions.explanation: Combine and list each element once: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.

questions.question: If B = {2, 4, 6, 8} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then B ∪ C =
questions.explanation: Combine: 2, 4, 6, 8 together with 3, 5 gives {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8}.

questions.question: If B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then B ∪ B =
questions.explanation: The union of a set with itself adds nothing: B ∪ B = B.

questions.question: The property (A ∪ B) ∪ C = A ∪ (B ∪ C), true for any three sets, is called the:
questions.explanation: Regrouping without changing order is the associative law.

questions.question: If S = {a, b, c, d} and T = {f, b, d, g}, then S ∪ T =
options: {a, b, c, d, f, b, d, g}
questions.explanation: Combine and list b and d once: {a, b, c, d, f, g}.

questions.question: If S = {a, b, c, d} and T = {f, b, d, g}, then S ∩ T =
questions.explanation: The common elements are b and d.

questions.question: If V = {2, 4, 6, …} (multiples of 2) and W = {3, 6, 9, …} (multiples of 3), then V ∩ W =
questions.explanation: Numbers that are multiples of both 2 and 3 are multiples of 6: {6, 12, 18, …}.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then A ∩ B =
questions.explanation: Common elements: 2 and 4.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then A ∩ C =
questions.explanation: Common elements: 3 and 4.

questions.question: If A and B are disjoint sets, then A ∩ B =
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets have no common element, so their intersection is empty: ∅.

questions.question: For any sets A and B, which of these is always true?
questions.explanation: Every element of A is in A ∪ B, so A ⊂ (A ∪ B). The others fail in general (e.g. A = {1}, B = {2}).

questions.question: The difference A − B is the set of elements that:
options: belong to B but not to A
belong to both A and B
belong to A but not to B
belong to neither A nor B
questions.explanation: A − B = { x | x ∈ A and x ∉ B }: elements that belong to A but not to B.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then A − B =
questions.explanation: Remove from A the elements that are in B (2 and 4): {1, 3}.

questions.question: If B = {2, 4, 6, 8} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then B − C =
questions.explanation: Remove from B the elements in C (4 and 6): {2, 8}.

questions.question: If R is the set of real numbers and Q the set of rational numbers, then R − Q consists of:
questions.explanation: Real numbers that are not rational are the irrational numbers.

questions.question: A − B can also be written as:
questions.explanation: x ∈ A and x ∉ B means x ∈ A and x ∈ B′, so A − B = A ∩ B′.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, …, 9} and A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, then A′ =
questions.explanation: A′ is everything in U not in A: {5, 6, 7, 8, 9}.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, …, 9}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then (A ∩ C)′ =
questions.explanation: A ∩ C = {3, 4}. Its complement in U is {1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9}.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, …, 9}, A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 4, 6, 8}, then (A ∪ B)′ =
questions.explanation: A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8}. Its complement in U is {5, 7, 9}.

questions.question: For any set A, the complement of the complement of A, written (A′)′, is:
questions.explanation: Taking the complement twice returns the original set: (A′)′ = A.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, …, 9}, B = {2, 4, 6, 8} and C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, then (B − C)′ =
questions.explanation: B − C = {2, 8}. Its complement in U is {1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9}.

questions.question: For any set A (with universal set U), A ∪ A′ =
questions.explanation: Every element of U is either in A or in A′, so A ∪ A′ = U.

questions.question: The complement of the universal set, U′, is:
questions.explanation: Nothing lies outside U, so U′ = ∅.

questions.question: If A is a subset of B, then A ∩ B =
questions.explanation: Every element of A is already in B, so the common part is A.

questions.question: If A is a subset of B, then A ∪ B =
questions.explanation: Everything in A is already in B, so the union is B.

questions.question: If A is a subset of B, then which of these is true?
questions.explanation: If x ∉ B then x ∉ A (since A ⊂ B). So every element of B′ is in A′, i.e. B′ ⊂ A′.

questions.question: If A is a subset of B, then A ∪ (B − A) =
questions.explanation: B − A is the part of B outside A. Adding A back gives all of B.

questions.question: For any set A, A ∩ ∅ =
questions.explanation: ∅ has no elements, so nothing can be common to A and ∅: A ∩ ∅ = ∅.

questions.question: The sets (A − B), (A ∩ B) and (B − A) are:
questions.explanation: No element can be in two of these regions at once, so the intersection of any two is empty: they are mutually disjoint.

questions.question: If n(A) = 20, n(B) = 15 and n(A ∩ B) = 5, then n(A ∪ B) =
In a class of 40 students, 25 offer Mathematics, 20 offer Physics and 10 offer both. How many students offer neither subject?
questions.explanation: Students offering at least one = 25 + 20 − 10 = 35. Neither = 40 − 35 = 5.

questions.question: On a Venn diagram, A ∪ B is represented by:
options: the part of A outside B
the whole area covered by both circles
questions.explanation: A ∪ B consists of everything in A, in B, or in both: both circles together.

questions.question: On a Venn diagram, A ∩ B is represented by:
options: the area common to both circles
the part of B outside A
questions.explanation: A ∩ B is the overlapping region of the two circles.

questions.question: On a Venn diagram with the universal set U drawn as a rectangle, the complement A′ is the area:
options: outside circle A but inside the rectangle
questions.explanation: A′ = U − A: everything in U that is outside circle A but inside the rectangle.

questions.question: The correct relationship between the sets of natural numbers (N), integers (Z), rational numbers (Q) and real numbers (R) is:
questions.explanation: Every natural number is an integer, every integer is rational (n = n/1), and every rational number is real: N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R.

questions.question: The set of integers is closed under:
questions.explanation: The sum, difference and product of integers are integers, but a quotient such as 3 ÷ 7 is not an integer. So the integers are closed under addition, subtraction and multiplication only.
